regen_doc:
## Registering a federated connection as a Glue Data Catalog

If you use AWS Glue Data Catalog federated connectors without Lambda, they are already registered as a Glue Data Catalog and work with fine-grained access control, so you can ignore this section.

After you create your data source, you can use the Athena console to register your connection as a Glue Data Catalog. Once a connection is registered as a Glue Data Catalog, you can manage your federated data catalog and enable fine-grained access control using Lake Formation. You can register the following connectors to integrate with AWS Glue for fine-grained access control: AWS CMDB, Timestream, Azure Data Lake Storage, Azure Synapse, IBM Db2, IBM Db2 AS/400 (Db2 iSeries), Google Cloud Storage, HBase, TPC-DS, Cloudera Hive, Cloudwatch, Cloudwatch Metrics, Vertica, BigQuery, DocumentDB, DynamoDB, MySQL, OpenSearch, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Redshift, SAP HANA, Snowflake, SQL Server, and Teradata.

### Prerequisites

Before you begin, you must have the roles and permissions needed to register locations, as well as the required Lake Formation roles. The role that you register in Glue must have the permissions listed in the example policy. That policy allows s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the spill bucket prefix resources, lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector function, and glue:* on the Glue connection and the catalog.

You are responsible for determining and managing the appropriate data access. With fine-grained access controls on federated queries, it is recommended that you use the AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy. If you use your own policy, you must ensure that users executing federated queries do not have access to any of the following: lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector specified in the Glue connection, spill bucket location access in IAM, access to the Glue connection associated with your federated catalog, or the Lake Formation role in IAM.

### Registering through the console

To register through the console, open the Athena console, choose **Data sources and catalogs**, choose the data source you created, and then choose **Get started with AWS Lake Formation**. After you make this choice, you must manage your Lambda function on your own. Athena will not delete your Lambda function when you register the connection as a Glue Data Catalog.

During registration, you must provide a unique name for your catalog as the **Data catalog name**. You must also choose a Lake Formation IAM role that grants permission to Lake Formation to invoke the Lambda function; this role must have the permissions shown in the example. Finally, you must type **confirm** to delete the Athena data source and replace it with a Glue data catalog registration. Registration deletes your Athena data source and creates a new Glue Data Catalog in its place.

Choosing **Create catalog and go to Lake Formation** opens the Lake Formation console, where you can manage the catalog and grant permissions to users on catalogs, databases and tables. After registration completes, you may need to update queries that access the data source to refer to the newly created Glue data catalog.

# Registering a federated connection as a Glue Data Catalog

## Before you begin

- Required Lake Formation roles and permissions for connecting the Data Catalog to external data sources. The steps are at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lake-formation/latest/dg/federated-catalog-data-connection.html.
- The roles and permissions needed to register locations.
- The role that you register in Glue, which must have the permissions listed in the example policy (described below).

AWS Glue Data Catalog federated connectors without Lambda are already registered as a Glue Data Catalog and work with fine-grained access control, so they can ignore this section.

## Overview

After you create your data source, you can use the Athena console to register your connection as a Glue Data Catalog. This holds only when you have the roles and permissions needed to register locations, have the required Lake Formation roles, and the role you register in Glue has the permissions in the example policy. Once a connection is registered as a Glue Data Catalog, you can manage your federated data catalog and enable fine-grained access control using Lake Formation.

You can register the following connectors to integrate with AWS Glue for fine-grained access control: AWS CMDB, Timestream, Azure Data Lake Storage, Azure Synapse, IBM Db2, IBM Db2 AS/400 (Db2 iSeries), Google Cloud Storage, HBase, TPC-DS, Cloudera Hive, Cloudwatch, Cloudwatch Metrics, Vertica, BigQuery, DocumentDB, DynamoDB, MySQL, OpenSearch, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Redshift, SAP HANA, Snowflake, SQL Server, and Teradata.

## Permissions and access responsibilities

The role that you register in Glue must have the permissions listed in the example policy. The example policy allows s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the spill bucket prefix resources, lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector function, and glue:* on the Glue connection and the catalog.

You are responsible for determining and managing the appropriate data access. With fine-grained access controls on federated queries, it is recommended that you use the AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy. If you use your own policy, you must ensure that users executing federated queries do not have access to lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector specified in the Glue connection, spill bucket location access in IAM, access to the Glue connection associated with your federated catalog, or the Lake Formation role in IAM.

## Register through the console

First, open the Athena console, choose Data sources and catalogs, choose the data source you created, and then choose Get started with AWS Lake Formation. This must happen before you supply the registration details below. After you choose Get started with AWS Lake Formation, you must manage your Lambda function on your own. Athena will not delete your Lambda function when you register the connection as a Glue Data Catalog.

Next, complete the following:

1. Provide a unique name for your catalog as the Data catalog name.
2. Choose a Lake Formation IAM role that grants permission to Lake Formation to invoke the Lambda function. The role must have the permissions shown in the example.
3. Type confirm to delete the Athena data source and replace it with a Glue data catalog registration.

Registration deletes your Athena data source and creates a new Glue Data Catalog in its place. As a result, after registration completes, you may need to update queries that access the data source to refer to the newly created Glue data catalog.

Finally, choose Create catalog and go to Lake Formation. This opens the Lake Formation console, where you can manage the catalog and grant permissions to users on catalogs, databases and tables. This works only when the catalog name, the Lake Formation IAM role, and the confirmation have all been provided, so complete all three of those before choosing it.

regen_doc:
## Registering a connection as a Glue Data Catalog

AWS Glue Data Catalog federated connectors that work without Lambda are already registered as a Glue Data Catalog and work with fine-grained access control, so if you use one of those, you can ignore this section.

For other connectors, after you create your data source, you can use the Athena console to register your connection as a Glue Data Catalog. Once a connection is registered as a Glue Data Catalog, you can manage your federated data catalog and enable fine-grained access control using Lake Formation. You can register the following connectors to integrate with AWS Glue for fine-grained access control: AWS CMDB, Timestream, Azure Data Lake Storage, Azure Synapse, IBM Db2, IBM Db2 AS/400 (Db2 iSeries), Google Cloud Storage, HBase, TPC-DS, Cloudera Hive, Cloudwatch, Cloudwatch Metrics, Vertica, BigQuery, DocumentDB, DynamoDB, MySQL, OpenSearch, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Redshift, SAP HANA, Snowflake, SQL Server, and Teradata.

### Prerequisites

Before you begin, you must have the roles and permissions needed to register locations, as well as the required Lake Formation roles. The role that you register in Glue must have the permissions listed in the example policy. That policy allows s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the spill bucket prefix resources, lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector function, and glue:* on the Glue connection and the catalog.

You are responsible for determining and managing the appropriate data access. With fine-grained access controls on federated queries, it is recommended that you use the AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy. If you use your own policy, you must ensure that users executing federated queries do not have access to any of the following: lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector specified in the Glue connection, spill bucket location access in IAM, the Glue connection associated with your federated catalog, or the Lake Formation role in IAM.

### Registering through the console

To register through the console, open the Athena console, choose **Data sources and catalogs**, choose the data source you created, and then choose **Get started with AWS Lake Formation**.

After you choose **Get started with AWS Lake Formation**, you must manage your Lambda function on your own. Athena will not delete your Lambda function when you register the connection as a Glue Data Catalog.

During registration, you must provide a unique name for your catalog as the **Data catalog name**. You must also choose a Lake Formation IAM role that grants permission to Lake Formation to invoke the Lambda function; the role must have the permissions shown in the example. Finally, you must type **confirm** to delete the Athena data source and replace it with a Glue data catalog registration. Registration deletes your Athena data source and creates a new Glue Data Catalog in its place. After registration completes, you may need to update queries that access the data source to refer to the newly created Glue data catalog.

Choosing **Create catalog and go to Lake Formation** opens the Lake Formation console, where you can manage the catalog and grant permissions to users on catalogs, databases, and tables.

# Registering a federated connection as a Glue Data Catalog

## Before you begin

Complete the following prerequisites before you start the registration steps.

- **Required Lake Formation roles.** Set up the Lake Formation roles required for connecting the Data Catalog to external data sources. The steps are at https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lake-formation/latest/dg/federated-catalog-data-connection.html. You must also have the roles and permissions needed to register locations.
- **Identity-based IAM policy.** Attach an identity-based IAM policy with glue, lambda and s3 permissions to the Lake Formation role. The steps are on this page. The role that you register in Glue must have the permissions listed in the example policy. That policy allows s3:ListBucket and s3:GetObject on the spill bucket prefix resources, allows lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector function, and allows glue:* on the Glue connection and the catalog.

## Who this section applies to

AWS Glue Data Catalog federated connectors without Lambda are already registered as a Glue Data Catalog and work with fine-grained access control, so they can ignore this section.

After you create your data source, you can use the Athena console to register your connection as a Glue Data Catalog. This works only when you hold the roles and permissions needed to register locations, the required Lake Formation roles, and the example-policy permissions on the role you register in Glue. Once a connection is registered as a Glue Data Catalog, you can manage your federated data catalog and enable fine-grained access control using Lake Formation.

You can register the following connectors to integrate with AWS Glue for fine-grained access control: AWS CMDB, Timestream, Azure Data Lake Storage, Azure Synapse, IBM Db2, IBM Db2 AS/400 (Db2 iSeries), Google Cloud Storage, HBase, TPC-DS, Cloudera Hive, Cloudwatch, Cloudwatch Metrics, Vertica, BigQuery, DocumentDB, DynamoDB, MySQL, OpenSearch, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Redshift, SAP HANA, Snowflake, SQL Server, and Teradata.

## Access management responsibilities

You are responsible for determining and managing the appropriate data access. With fine-grained access controls on federated queries, it is recommended that you use the AmazonAthenaFullAccess managed policy. If you use your own policy, you must ensure that users executing federated queries do not have any of the following:

- access to lambda:InvokeFunction on the Lambda connector specified in the Glue connection;
- spill bucket location access in IAM;
- access to the Glue connection associated with your federated catalog;
- the Lake Formation role in IAM.

## Register through the console

Open the Athena console, choose **Data sources and catalogs**, choose the data source you created, and then choose **Get started with AWS Lake Formation**.

After you choose Get started with AWS Lake Formation, you must manage your Lambda function on your own. Athena will not delete your Lambda function when you register the connection as a Glue Data Catalog.

In the registration form, complete the following:

1. Provide a unique name for your catalog as the **Data catalog name**.
2. Choose a Lake Formation IAM role that grants permission to Lake Formation to invoke the Lambda function. The role must have the permissions shown in the example.
3. Type **confirm** to delete the Athena data source and replace it with a Glue data catalog registration.

Typing confirm must happen before registration proceeds, because registration deletes your Athena data source and creates a new Glue Data Catalog in its place. Because of this replacement, after registration completes you may need to update queries that access the data source to refer to the newly created Glue data catalog.

Choosing **Create catalog and go to Lake Formation** is possible only when the unique catalog name, the Lake Formation IAM role, and the typed confirmation are all in place, and you must complete all three before you choose it. It opens the Lake Formation console, where you can manage the catalog and grant permissions to users on catalogs, databases and tables.
